title: Your portfolio needs a decision, not another certificate
subtitle: Give someone a reason to trust how you think.
coverAlt: A laptop with a dashboard on a sunlit desk
resourceReason: Use The Better Brief to scope a small portfolio project, explain your choices and decide what to leave out.
body:
Suppose you finish a course on product design. You have a certificate, a folder of exercises and a portfolio page waiting for something to go on it. So you open a design file and start making a very beautiful banking app.

By Sunday, there are seventeen screens. You have chosen the font, the colours and the little animation after a transfer. You have not decided whose banking problem you are solving.

Seventeen screens is a lot of work. It is also a lot to ask someone to look through when the reason for making them is missing.

I’d rather see one screen with a good reason behind it.

Start with a small problem

A course gives you exercises. Your own project needs a question. Take something ordinary enough to investigate without permission from a large company: finding a local class, comparing delivery charges, or booking an appointment that keeps getting rearranged.

Pick one. Write down who has the problem, what they do now and which part you want to understand. If you have spoken to nobody yet, say so. An assumption does not become a finding because it is written inside a nice rectangle.

You can use tools to organise notes, draft questions or make a first screen quickly. That leaves you with more time to check the part you were guessing about. The tool cannot turn an invented interview into a real conversation.

Show the choice you made

Suppose your appointment page originally lets people choose a date before seeing the price. You decide to put the price first because people need to know what they are agreeing to.

That is something to write about. Explain the old order, the new order and what would convince you to change it again. A hiring manager can now read how you made a decision, rather than trying to infer it from a screenshot.

Keep the rejected version too. Two options and a reason for choosing one tell a better story than a final design presented as if it arrived fully formed.

If you test it, describe the test honestly. Three friends completing a task is a small test with three friends. It is not proof that the whole market wants your product. If you have not tested it, write the task you intend to test and the result you would watch for.

Finish something someone can inspect

A working link helps. So does a short explanation that survives without you standing beside it. Put the problem, your decisions and the remaining questions where a visitor can find them.

For a design, show a usable flow. For research, share a brief with sources. For a small tool, let someone try one task and understand what happens to their input. Keep private information out of the public version.

You do not need to claim that a weekend project changed an industry. You need to make it possible for someone to see the work and judge it.

The certificate can stay. Just give it some company: a small piece of work where your decisions are visible.

title: Before you build the app, take one order
subtitle: A business can teach you something before it has a login screen.
coverAlt: A green-screen laptop beside plants on a warm wooden desk
resourceReason: Keep customer questions, source notes and findings together in the Research Notebook before committing to an app.
body:
Consider a lunch delivery idea for a small office. The first plan includes an app, restaurant profiles, payment accounts and a dashboard for riders. There is even a loyalty programme. Nobody has ordered lunch yet.

I understand the temptation. Making the app feels like starting the business. A screen gives you something to show people, and now it is easier to make that screen without hiring a whole team.

But the unanswered question is still sitting there: will anyone order this lunch, at this price, under these conditions?

Make the first order possible

For a small trial, the first version can be a menu, a clear order deadline and a way to confirm an order. A form or a message is enough if you can handle it reliably.

Choose one office and one delivery window. Tell customers what is available, what it costs and what happens if an item runs out. Check the requirements that apply to preparing and selling food before taking payment. An experiment still has to treat people properly.

Keep the trial small enough that you can deliver what you promise. Taking forty orders is not useful evidence if you only have the capacity for ten.

Write down what happens

Suppose someone asks to pay after delivery. Another person wants lunch later than the chosen window. A third person opens the menu and leaves without ordering. These are different questions, and they deserve different notes.

Ask about the last time they bought lunch, rather than asking if your idea sounds nice. Where did they order? What did they pay? What went wrong? Record the answer and the date. Keep their personal details private.

Separate something a customer said from your explanation of it. “I finish my meeting at two” is a note. “Everyone needs late delivery” is a conclusion you have not earned.

Record the work on your side too. Time spent confirming orders, checking payment, replacing sold-out meals and finding the right entrance all belongs in your understanding of the business. A tidy checkout page does not remove any of those jobs.

Build around a repeated problem

After a few small trials, suppose people keep choosing from the same short menu, but the back-and-forth about available meals takes too long. You now have a reason to make a page that shows current availability.

If confirmations are the difficult part, work on those. If the delivery window does not fit customers’ working day, another feature will not fix the schedule.

There is no rule that the manual version must last forever. It lets you learn which work is worth turning into software and which work needs a different business decision.

You can still build the app. You will have actual orders, questions and mistakes to guide what goes into it. And if the first few trials tell you that this particular lunch service should not exist, that is a useful thing to learn before designing the loyalty programme.

title: The task you should stop doing twice
subtitle: Before you automate it, decide what should happen when it goes wrong.
coverAlt: A laptop showing charts on a quiet white desk
resourceReason: Use Before You Ship to check the inputs, failure states and recovery path of your first small automation.
body:
Suppose every Friday you copy bookings from a form into a spreadsheet. Then you send a confirmation to each person, mark the row and check that you did not send anything twice.

It takes forty minutes. The job is boring enough that you start thinking about an automation. Sensible. But copying the task into a tool is only part of the work.

The moment a message is sent automatically, a small mistake can reach somebody before you notice it. I’d want to understand the task before giving it that freedom.

Write the boring details

What makes a booking ready for confirmation? A completed form is not always the same as a confirmed place. There can be missing details, a full session or a payment still being checked.

Write down the conditions. Then write down what the automation is allowed to change. In this example, it reads a booking, checks the conditions, sends one confirmation and records that it did so. It should not quietly approve every row.

That short description gives you something to check against the finished tool. It also tells you which jobs still belong to a person.

Keep a record of each run

A completed run should leave a record you can read: which booking it handled, when it ran and what happened. Avoid copying personal information into logs when a booking reference will do.

If the tool stops halfway through, you need to know which messages have already gone out. Restarting from the beginning without checking can send the same confirmation again.

Use a separate reference for each booking and check for an existing confirmation before sending another. Test that behaviour with fake records first. The test is cheap; apologising to twenty people is less pleasant.

Plan for the failed run

A connection can drop. A service can refuse a request. Someone can enter an email address incorrectly. Decide which failures should stop the run and which ones should leave a row for a person to review.

Make failure visible. A tool that quietly skips an order is not saving you work. It is leaving you with a problem you cannot see.

Start with a review step before any real messages go out. Compare the proposed confirmations with the spreadsheet. Once the results are consistently correct, decide if automatic sending is appropriate for this particular task.

Give yourself an off switch

You should be able to pause the automation without dismantling it. Keep the manual way of doing the job documented too, including where the latest records live.

The aim is to spend less time repeating a task while keeping control of what happens. A small automation that does one job reliably is enough.

Try it with a few fake bookings: a valid one, a duplicate, an incomplete one and a failed delivery. If you can explain where each ends up, you are ready to review a small live trial.

title: The prompt isn’t the thinking
subtitle: A very confident answer still needs a good question.
coverAlt: An open notebook being written in beside a cup of coffee
resourceReason: Try Ask Better’s 18 prompts for research, decisions and critique. They ask for missing evidence as well as answers.
body:
Ask an AI tool for ten business ideas and you can get a neat list in seconds. Ask it to rank the list and it can do that too. By the third reply, one idea has a name, a tagline and a plan for launch.

All very satisfying. Nobody has spoken to a customer.

The speed is useful. It is also easy to mistake the amount of text produced for the amount you now know. I’d slow down at the moment the tool starts making decisions on information it does not have.

Tell it what you actually know

Suppose you want to help independent tutors arrange lessons. You have spoken to two tutors, both of whom spend time rescheduling. You do not know how often it happens, what they use now or if they would pay to solve it.

Put those limits in the prompt. Ask the tool to separate the information you supplied from assumptions it is making. Ask what questions would help you choose the next step.

The response is now something you can use to prepare a conversation. It is not a report proving that tutors need your product. Two conversations are still two conversations.

Ask for the missing information

“Make this idea better” gives the tool permission to add features. “Which assumptions would change this decision if they were wrong?” asks it to do a different job.

For the tutoring idea, the useful questions concern the frequency of cancellations, who requests changes and how tutors recover the lost time. A new logo will not answer them.

You can ask for several explanations of the same problem. Then write down what evidence would help you choose between them. That gives you an actual research task, rather than another list of suggestions.

Check anything you plan to repeat

If the answer includes a statistic, a quote or a claim about a company, find the original source and read it. A reference on its own is not enough. Check the date, the group it describes and the limits of the claim.

If you cannot verify it, do not use it as support for your decision. Keep it as a question to investigate or leave it out.

Protect the people whose information you are working with. Do not paste private interview notes or customer records into a tool without the right permission and data controls. You can describe a problem without sharing someone’s name and phone number.

Keep your own decision in the document

After using the tool, write a few sentences yourself: what you are choosing, what you know, what you are assuming and what would make you reconsider.

If those sentences are difficult to write, you have found the work that still needs doing. Another polished reply will not complete it for you.

Use the speed to ask more precise questions and try a small version sooner. You still get to decide which answer deserves to become an actual thing.

title: You don’t need a new app to learn something
subtitle: Give yourself one small thing to make with what you learn.
coverAlt: A woman reading a book in a sunny room
resourceReason: Use the Research Notebook to keep a question, sources and your own notes together while you practise a new skill.
body:
Suppose you decide to learn data analysis. You save a course, join a community, choose a note-taking app and spend an evening making the dashboard where you will track your progress.

The dashboard looks excellent. You have not opened a dataset.

Getting organised feels like doing the work because it takes time and produces something visible. But it is possible to organise a subject very carefully without getting any better at it. I’d give the learning a task before giving it another app.

Choose something you want to understand

For data analysis, take a small public dataset with a source and a date. Ask one question it can reasonably answer. How has a measure changed over time? Which entries are missing? Are you comparing things measured in the same way?

Keep the question narrow enough to attempt with the skills you have. You do not need to finish a whole course before looking at ten rows.

For writing, the task can be explaining a difficult idea in a short paragraph. For design, it can be helping someone finish one booking. You are giving the lesson somewhere to be used.

Make an attempt before asking for the answer

Try the exercise yourself. Write down where you got stuck and what you expected to happen. Then use a lesson, a person or an AI tool to help with that particular point.

When asking a tool, request an explanation of the step you do not understand. Ask for a small example you can change. Running a complete answer successfully does not tell you if you understand why it works.

Keep the first attempt. Comparing it with the next one tells you more than a tick beside “studied today.” You can see the mistake, the correction and the question that remains.

Check that you can do it again

Use different inputs or explain the method without looking at your notes. For the dataset, change the date range and check if you can still describe the calculation. For writing, explain another idea using the same constraint.

If you cannot, return to the part that is unclear. That is a precise reason to revisit a lesson. You do not need to restart the course or buy a different one.

A small test is enough to tell you what to practise next. It does not need a score, a leaderboard or a public announcement.

Keep less, use more

A source list helps when you can find the thing you need again. A notebook helps when it contains your own explanation alongside any copied paragraphs. Keep the link, a short note and the question it helped answer.

Choose a simple place for those records and stick with it long enough to do some work. If the setup starts taking more time than the exercise, close the settings.

Your next task is allowed to be small. Open the dataset. Write the paragraph. Try the booking flow. Give yourself something you can look at tomorrow and say, “I understand this part better now.”
